extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Popular Science Monthly (educated lay public, scientists and clinicians, late 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for observing and interpreting muscular signs as expressions of nervous-system states (diagnostic clinical observation of nerve-muscular expression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific rule: deduce only from established facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce no principle which facts will not prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers and scientific workers should not draw general principles unless supported by reliable facts; avoid building social reforms on insufficiently proved scientific inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in using brain-weight data
rubrics_metrics.description: Students of physiology see that a final and conclusive law cannot yet be drawn from differences in brain-weights and measurements, because of the present imperfection of such data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological measurements (e.g., cranial capacity, brain weights) are informative but currently imperfect; use them cautiously and supplement with broader evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain weight/size as an index of capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The general superiority, in absolute weight, of the male over the female brain exists at every period of development (male mean ≈ 49½ oz; female mean ≈ 44 oz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical brain-weight ranges and averages are used as evidence that size correlates with capacity; beware of inferring qualitative differences solely from weight but consider weight as an important quantitative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge brain-power by brain-products
rubrics_metrics.description: We have a right to insist on the legitimacy of judging brain-power by brain-products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the external products/results of brain activity (works produced, accomplishments) as evidence of cognitive capacity, analogous to judging muscle by work done or looms by manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of power proportional to body size
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of power is in proportion to the size of the body; matter and force are inseparable — a large amount of matter represents more force than a small amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing capacities between individuals or sexes, account for differences in body and organ size as primary determinants of potential energetic output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy derived from food equals available power
rubrics_metrics.description: All human energy is derived from the food, and is an exact equivalent of the amount of food consumed and assimilated; men assimilate about twenty per cent more food than women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use food-assimilation as a proxy for available physiological energy; differences in assimilation imply differences in total available power for bodily and mental work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-factor in cognitive output
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of larger organs and greater circulating blood per unit time, a man will do more thinking in an hour than a woman — the time-factor gives larger organisms a permanent advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating cognitive performance, consider not only total capacity but rate (amount of work/time); larger bodies/brains may process more within the same time interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maternity diverts female energy affecting intellectual development
rubrics_metrics.description: Probably twenty per cent of the energy of women between twenty and forty years of age is diverted for the maintenance of maternity and its attendant exactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for reproductive biological costs (pregnancy, childrearing) when comparing average energetic availability for sustained intellectual development between sexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heredity and sexual selection affect transmission of intellectual traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of heredity and sex-differential transmission (Darwin, Spencer) may increase intellectual endowment in the male; intellectual mothers may have fewer daughters, reducing female-line transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evolutionary and hereditary mechanisms (including differential transmission and reproduction patterns) as long-term influences on population-level differences in intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as a distinct faculty with lower-order associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers of intuition, rapid perception, and imitation are more strongly marked in women; these faculties are closely akin to instinct and characteristic of lower races and a past state of civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intuition/rapid perception as different in kind from reasoning and creative imagination; the author argues it is a less complex/advanced form and should be weighed accordingly when assessing cognitive 'quality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Movements reflect nerve-centre states
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements depend upon nerve-muscular stimuli originating in nerve-centers; muscular conditions are expressions of the states of those centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinicians should interpret observed movements (attitude, gait, gestures, reflexes) as indicators of underlying brain or spinal-cord states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use muscular observation to judge nervous system condition
rubrics_metrics.description: We commonly judge of the state of the nervous system by muscular conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe posture, gait, tremor, reflexes, and other muscular phenomena systematically to infer nervous-system health or pathology; include comparisons between rested and fatigued states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stooping attitude and spiritless gait indicate fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: Note the stooping attitude and spiritless gait of a tired man as compared with that of the same individual when rested and refreshed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use changes in posture and gait across states (rested vs. fatigued) as simple diagnostic signs of tiredness vs normal function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reeling gait, unsteady hand, tremor indicate incipient intoxication
rubrics_metrics.description: Incipient intoxication is indicated by a reeling gait, unsteady hand, and muscular tremor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific motor signs are standard clinical indicators of early alcohol/drug intoxication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head position and asymmetrical gestures signal emotional or nervous states
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of the head: firmly upright in defiance, drooping in shame; commonly held on one side in nervous women and girls convalescent from chorea (asymmetrical gesture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret habitual head carriage and asymmetries as expressive of emotional states or residual neurological conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic/musical motor skills reflect trained brain condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist's brush or pencil, the sculptor's modeling-tool and chisel, the pianist's and violinist's finger-touch, indicate the training and actual condition of the working of his brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-skilled, refined motor patterns are indicative of specific training and underlying neural organization — use them as evidence of functional brain condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant reflexes and movements indicate nervous-system health
rubrics_metrics.description: In the infant the condition of the nervous system is best recorded in terms of nerve-muscular phenomena: it laughs, is playful; reflex action is well marked when a finger is placed in the child's mouth; the eyes are moved and directed toward any object looked at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess developmental reflexes and spontaneous movements in infants as primary signs of normal or abnormal nervous-system function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific convulsive motor sign: clenched fists with thumbs turned in
rubrics_metrics.description: In the convulsive state the fists are often closed, with the thumbs turned in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this stereotyped hand posture as one diagnostic sign among others when evaluating convulsive disorders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal associated eye movements and signs of their loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal movements of the eye include pupil responses, accommodation, and coordinated turning; loss of associated movements may be seen in deep anaesthesia from chloroform, in coma from alcoholism, or in profound sleep of infants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test coordinated ocular movements and pupil responses; presence of strabismus, unequal movements, or pinpoint-contracted pupils with loss of parallelism indicate severe central depression (e.g., anaesthesia, coma, meningitis) and tend to reverse with returning consciousness.
